prot-099.title: The Huainan worms
prot-099.text: Some of the first creatures you could see without a microscope lived in what is now China. Near Huainan City, in Anhui, small worm-shaped organisms large enough to see with the naked eye record a transitional stage in evolution, 840–740 million years ago. A similar biota, about 1 billion years old, was found on Russia's Timan Ridge. Both hint that life was moving from microbes toward larger, more complex forms.

arch-010.title: The oldest banded iron formations
arch-010.text: Rocks striped in rust and silica record a world almost without oxygen. Banded iron formations are made of thin alternating layers rich in iron and in silica. The oldest known lie at Isua, in Greenland's greenstone belt, and date from about 3,800–3,700 million years ago. Their iron isotopes point to extremely low oxygen and to iron oxidized by {{ref:arch-013}}. Iron formations of this Algoma type formed mainly in the Archean, and deposition later peaked near the eon's end.

arch-009.title: Greenland's Isua Greenstone Belt
arch-009.text: Pillows of lava in Greenland prove there was water to erupt into. The Isua belt was built from volcanic and sedimentary layers about 3,800 and 3,700 million years old. It is the largest exposure on Earth of Eoarchean supracrustal rock, rock formed at the surface. Its pillow basalt formed in an underwater eruption, so liquid water existed 3.8 billion years ago. How the belt formed, by plate tectonics or by heat-pipe or plume volcanism, is still contentious.

arch-017.title: India's Dharwar Craton forms
arch-017.text: The oldest part of the Indian peninsula was built by ocean floor sinking and melting. India's Dharwar Craton formed between 3.6 and 2.5 billion years ago. Around 3350 million years ago, ridge push drove oceanic crust down into the mantle. The melting slab produced its TTG crust of tonalite, trondhjemite and granodiorite, light granite-like rocks. Its three blocks joined between 2560 and 2500 million years ago, closing all of its subduction zones, where one plate dives beneath another.

arch-027.title: A nitrogen sky with almost no oxygen
arch-027.text:
A visitor to the Archean would have suffocated. By about 3.4 billion years ago, nitrogen was the main gas of a stable second atmosphere that also held methane, carbon dioxide, water vapor and sulfur gases. Volcanic outgassing made it, with extra gases from huge asteroids of the Late Heavy Bombardment.

It was anoxic and weakly reducing. Oxygen stayed around or below 0.001% of today's level until about 2.4 billion years ago. Any oxygen made by early photosynthesis was quickly used up oxidizing iron, sulfur and methane. Sulfur-isotope signals rule out significant oxygen before about 2.45 billion years ago. River and delta grains of pyrite, siderite and uraninite older than 2.4 billion years tell the same story, since these minerals break down in oxygen.

arch-039.title: When did plate tectonics begin?
arch-039.text:
The ground beneath your feet moves a few centimeters a year, but when did it start moving? A possible onset of plate tectonics is placed around 3 billion years ago, yet its timing is still debated.

The Mesoarchean holds the first evidence of modern-style subduction, where one plate dives beneath another. It includes an oceanic arc, a chain of volcanoes over a sinking plate, at a Pilbara convergent margin about 3.12 billion years ago. Diamonds add more clues. Minerals trapped in them suggest the supercontinent cycle, the repeated gathering and breakup of continents, began roughly 3 billion years ago. Diamonds from crustal eclogite became common after 3.0 billion.

Earlier, the picture differs. A hotter Paleoarchean mantle ruled out modern plate tectonics, and some suggest a stagnant lid, a single unbroken shell, instead. Other estimates range from the Hadean, over 4 billion years ago, to 2.2 billion years, or just 800 million years for fully modern-style tectonics. The debate links back to {{ref:hade-004}}.

arch-060.title: Stromatolite reefs spread
arch-060.text: Microbes built the world's first reefs. Stromatolites occur throughout the Archean. From about 2,700 million years ago they became a major part of the fossil record, common late in the eon. The earliest of confirmed microbial origin is 2.724 billion years old. In Zimbabwe, stromatolites of the Bulawayo series formed the first verified reef community on Earth.

arch-063.title: Carbonate platforms grow in the Transvaal
arch-063.text: Microbes built limestone shelves the size of seas. Between about 2.640 and 2.516 billion years ago, stromatolites built two successive carbonate platforms in the Transvaal Basin on the Kaapvaal craton. These are thick shelves of limy rock in shallow water. The oldest known giant carbonate platform dates from about 2,600 million years ago, and a rising Transvaal sea flooded tidal flats about 2.550 billion years ago.

prot-022.title: The Francevillian disks of Gabon
prot-022.text:
Strange disks up to 17 cm across lie flattened in Gabon's black shales. They come from the Francevillian B Formation, about 2.1 billion years old. Some authors read them as the earliest multicellular life and the earliest eukaryotes. A 2023 isotope study found an enrichment in light zinc that could reflect eukaryotic metabolism.

Whether they are fossils at all is disputed. A 2017 review called their biological origin questionable. A 2023 review suggested they may be artifacts of diagenesis, the chemical changes that turn sediment into rock. Recent reviews lean toward a non-biological origin.

prot-042.title: Banded iron formations disappear
prot-042.text:
After more than a billion years, the striped iron rocks suddenly stop. Banded iron formations largely vanish from the rock record worldwide after 1.85 billion years ago. Their end is read as the oxygenation of the deep ocean, once the iron dissolved in seawater had been oxidized and dropped out.

Before then, the ocean was persistently iron-rich, with possible intervals of euxinia, oxygen-free water laced with sulfide. The only extensive iron formations laid down later are tied to Cryogenian glacial deposits. An odd coincidence marks the turning point. A 10 km asteroid struck water about 1,000 m deep 1.849 billion years ago, just as iron-formation deposition paused.

prot-050.title: The Boring Billion
prot-050.text:
For about a billion years, Earth seemed to hold its breath. The Boring Billion, or Earth's Middle Ages, is an informal span from about 1.8 to 0.8 billion years ago. It was marked by tectonic stability, climatic stasis and slow biological evolution.

Oxygen stayed very low and no glaciations occurred, though a Scottish lake froze over in winter 1 billion years ago. The oceans may have been oxygen-poor, sulfidic and starved of nutrients, ruled by purple bacteria that used hydrogen sulfide instead of water, a so-called Canfield ocean. The carbon isotope record shows no major excursions. Mesoproterozoic temperatures may have averaged about 19 °C, some 4 °C warmer than today. The span ended with the breakup of Rodinia, a second oxygenation event and the Cryogenian Snowball Earth.

prot-075.title: The Grand Canyon Supergroup
prot-075.text: Deep in the Grand Canyon, tilted layers record an ancient seafloor. Nine formations of the Grand Canyon Supergroup were laid down in a sea between 1.2 billion and 740 million years ago. The Chuar Group formed in coastal and shallow seas. Its oldest layer, averaging 1250 million years, is the oldest in the canyon with fossils, stromatolites. The Cardenas Basalt, 1070 ± 70 million years old, tops the Unkar Group. About 800 million years ago the Grand Canyon orogeny tilted the supergroup 15° and broke it into fault blocks.

prot-084.title: Bangiomorpha, the first known sexual organism
prot-084.text:
The oldest evidence of sex comes from a tiny red seaweed in the Canadian Arctic. Bangiomorpha pubescens, a multicellular red alga from Somerset Island, closely resembles the living red alga Bangia.

Its differentiated reproductive cells are the oldest evidence of sexual reproduction and of meiosis, the cell division that makes sex cells with half the usual set of genes. It is also the earliest known organism that certainly had differentiated, specialized cells. And it is the oldest belonging to a living phylum, one of the major branches of life.

Why does it matter? Sex mixes the genes of two parents, so it increased genetic variation. That variation sped up evolution and the diversification of eukaryotes. The boom described in {{ref:prot-087}} may owe something to this small alga.

prot-093.title: Bitter Springs microfossils
prot-093.text: Some fossils are so well preserved that their insides still show. Cherts of Australia's Bitter Springs Group preserve stromatolites and exceptionally well-preserved cyanobacteria in silica. Some fossils with ghostly internal structures, such as Glenobotrydion, have been read as green algae, among the earliest plants, though that claim is debated. This style of preservation ended in the late Neoproterozoic, when organisms that secrete silica appeared.

prot-077.title: The Stac Fada impact and its missing crater
prot-077.text: An asteroid left its debris behind but hid its crater. The Stac Fada Member, a layer of rock, records an impact about 1.2 billion years ago. From that layer, geologists infer a crater about 40 km wide. Yet the crater itself has never been found, so the impact is known only from the debris it scattered.

prot-090.title: The late Ruker orogeny under Antarctic ice
prot-090.text: Antarctica hides a mountain range beneath its ice, and it may be a billion years old. Around 1 billion years ago, a mountain-building event, also called the Nimrod orogeny, struck the continent. It may have begun the Gamburtsev mountain range and the Vostok Subglacial Highlands, hidden today beneath the ice. Its date is uncertain by about 150 million years either way.

prot-071.title: Rodinia assembles
prot-071.text:
The broken pieces of one supercontinent came back together as another. Fragments of Columbia, scattered by {{ref:prot-063}}, accreted and collided to form Rodinia, which assembled between 1.26 and 0.90 billion years ago.

Laurentia, the ancient core of North America, sat at its center. Around it, Rodinia grew into the largest landmass yet, joining North American, East European, Amazonian, West African, Antarctic, Australian and Chinese blocks. Baltica and Amazonia collided with Laurentia in the Grenville, Sveconorwegian and Sunsás orogenies, between 1.1 and 0.9 billion years ago.

A single global ocean, Mirovia, surrounded it. Later, the proto-Pacific Panthalassa grew at Mirovia's expense.

For all its size, Rodinia remains shadowy. Its configuration and history are much less well understood than those of later supercontinents. Its later breakup, in {{ref:prot-108}}, would matter just as much as its assembly.

prot-041.title: Viruses that prey on bacteria
prot-041.text: Viruses are among life's oldest companions. Bacteriophages, viruses that infect bacteria, emerged before, or soon after, the lineages of prokaryotes and eukaryotes diverged. Prokaryotes are cells without a nucleus; eukaryotes have one. Their emergence is dated to about 1.85 billion years ago. That makes bacterial viruses nearly as old as the great division of cellular life itself.

prot-068.title: The Kibaran orogeny in Africa
prot-068.text: Central Africa's mountain belts record a very long collision. A series of Kibaran orogenic events ran from about 1,400 million years ago until about 1,000 million, when Rodinia was assembled. From 1.4 to 1.2 billion years ago, it fused the Tanzanian and Congo cratons. In a narrower sense, the name covers an event about 1,375 million years ago that formed the Karagwe-Ankolean belt.

arch-057.title: The oceans run short of nickel
arch-057.text: A shortage of one metal may have tipped the balance toward oxygen. From 2.7 to 2.4 billion years ago, nickel deposition fell steadily from 400 times today's level. Methane-making microbes need nickel. As volcanic nickel dwindled, oxygen producers began to outcompete them. The balance between the two kinds of microbe shifted toward oxygen.

arch-041.title: The Pongola glaciation, Earth's first known ice age
arch-041.text:
In a warm Archean world, ice suddenly appears in the rocks of southern Africa. The Pongola glaciation, from about 2.985 to 2.837 billion years ago, is the oldest known glaciation on Earth.

Its traces are diamictites, jumbled mixtures of boulders and mud dropped by glaciers, in the Mozaan Formation of the Pongola Supergroup. They crop out in KwaZulu-Natal and Eswatini.

The cold was an interruption. The Mesoarchean climate was otherwise warm or temperate, kept mild by high methane and carbon dioxide, as in {{ref:arch-033}}. Ice reached a palaeolatitude, an ancient latitude, of 48 degrees. Whether it pushed further toward the tropics is uncertain.

What cooled the planet? No one knows for sure. Sulfur-isotope changes suggest a link to an early, short-lived oxygenation of the atmosphere, described in {{ref:arch-042}}. If so, the first ice age on record was tied to the first stirrings of oxygen.
